strengths: Novel and creative core idea: leveraging the in-context/continuation log-probability of a pretrained LALM to define MCLP, a dense, interpretable, likelihood-based proxy for stylistic consistency in RP-TTS, which is a genuinely new angle compared to discrete emotion-classifier rewards.

The hybrid gated reward (MCLP style term + CER content penalty with a tolerance gate) is well-motivated, and the ablation in Table 3 empirically demonstrates reward hacking under single-objective optimization (style-only → CER >50%; content-only → flat prosody), which is an informative finding.

Substantial dataset contribution: ~1,435 hours / ~311k annotated scenes derived from real dramas with scene and character annotations, plus a clearly described multi-stage curation/annotation pipeline (Demucs separation, pyannote diarization, LLM-based profiling) and a video-level train/test split to avoid leakage.
The human-metric consistency analysis (Figure 5) provides at least some empirical validation that ΔMCLP tracks human MOS preferences, with a plausible monotone trend above ΔMCLP > 0.1.
Ablation studies reasonably isolate the SFT and RL stages, and the fair SFT-vs-RL comparison in Table 3 shows RL genuinely improves both style (MCLP) and content (CER/WER) over the SFT baseline.
weaknesses: The headline comparison in Table 2 is not apples-to-apples: 'Our Proposed' is fine-tuned (SFT+RL) on the in-domain RP-TTS dataset, while GPT-Audio, MiMo-Audio, and Step-Audio-2-mini are used without such domain tuning. The claim of 'significantly outperforming strong LALM baselines' is therefore inflated; the fairer SFT-vs-RL evidence in Table 3 is buried, and a fine-tuned-baseline comparison is missing.

MCLP is reported as '-' for GPT-Audio in Table 2, revealing that the metric is not computable across models with different tokenizers/architectures (it relies on TA4 tokens and a specific LALM). This is a fundamental limitation for a metric proposed as a general evaluation tool, yet it is never discussed. Moreover, MCLP is computed by the same model family (Step-Audio) used for generation, which may bias the score in its own favor.

The Information-Theoretic Analysis (Sec. 4.1) is loose/incorrect: the relation E[MCLP] ≈ -H(Z^gt|Z^eval) + D_KL(P_data||P_θ) conflates model and data distributions and is not rigorously derived, and the key assumption that MI variation is 'dominated by style' (because transcripts match) is asserted rather than shown. MCLP may equally capture timbre, channel conditions, or recording quality.

No statistical significance or variance is reported for the objective metrics (CER/WER/MCLP). The MCLP gaps between methods are small (~0.1–0.2 in log-prob), so practical significance is unclear and could be within noise.

Subjective evaluation rests on a very small sample (31 items, 30 valid responses) and the reported baseline MOS values (1.7–2.5) are unusually low and unexplained, raising concerns about the annotation setup or the stimulus selection.

Reproducibility gaps: the dataset is only promised to be 'open source,' the 'internal style classification model' used for RL filtering is not described, and the pretraining of the MCLP scorer (300w hours) and its relationship to the generation model are under-specified.

Ethics/legal considerations of building a role-play dataset from scraped YouTube dramas (copyright, consent, impersonation of real characters) are not addressed; the impact statement is boilerplate and does not engage with these issues.

Presentation/reference quality is sloppy: e.g., DeepSeek-R1 is cited as 'Guo et al., 2023' and 'Guo et al., 2025,' several references have mismatched years (Chen et al. 2024 vs. 2026, Shao et al. 2023 vs. 2024), and the terminology 'reverse continuation likelihood' is non-standard.

strengths: The paper tackles a genuinely under-served problem: evaluating and optimizing stylistic (non-emotional, persona-driven) consistency in multi-turn Role-Play TTS, where existing emotion-classification rewards and CER/SS metrics are indeed insufficient.

It attempts a unified metric-plus-reward pipeline (MCLP as both an objective score and a GRPO reward, gated by a CER constraint), which is a sensible engineering direction and is grounded in a concrete dataset-construction effort (~1,435 h, 311k annotated scenes with scene/character descriptions).
A human study was conducted (32 annotators) and an explicit reward-hacking ablation is reported, which is more than many comparable papers provide.
weaknesses: Circular and non-independent evaluation. MCLP is computed with a pretrained LALM of the same family (Step-Audio-2-mini-Base) that is then SFT/RL-optimized, and the same metric is used to evaluate the result. The metric, the reward, and the model therefore share the same probabilistic prior, so 'improvement' on MCLP is at least partly self-referential and cannot be treated as independent evidence.

The paper's own ablation refutes the central claim. In Table 3, the style-only variant attains the *highest* MCLP (-4.590) while CER explodes to >50% ('expressive gibberish'). If MCLP truly measured stylistic consistency, gibberish should not maximize it. This is direct counter-evidence that MCLP captures style, yet it is repackaged as an argument for the method rather than treated as a validity failure of the metric.

The metric has almost no discriminative resolution. In Table 2 all MCLP values lie within ~0.21 nats (-4.849 to -4.636), and the claimed 'significant' gains are ΔMCLP ≈ 0.05–0.09. Figure 5 itself shows that in exactly this small-ΔMCLP regime the win rate is only ~0.5–0.7 (near chance); meaningful correlation (win rate > 0.8) only appears for ΔMCLP > 0.1, a range the models under comparison essentially never reach. So by the authors' own analysis, MCLP is weakly informative for the differences being reported.

The information-theoretic justification is technically incorrect. Eq. (3) writes E[log P_θ(z^gt|z^eval)] ≈ −H(Z^gt|Z^eval) + D_KL(P_data‖P_θ). The standard cross-entropy identity gives E[log P_θ] = −H(P_data) − D_KL(P_data‖P_θ), i.e. the KL term enters with a *negative* sign. The derivation that 'assuming KL is small, higher MCLP ⇒ lower conditional entropy ⇒ higher MI' is therefore built on a sign error, weakening the theoretical support for the metric.

The main comparison is unfair. Baselines (GPT-Audio, MiMo-Audio-7B-Instruct, Step-Audio-2-mini) are off-the-shelf models, whereas the proposed system is SFT- and RL-trained on the authors' in-domain RP-TTS data. The SFT-only baseline is relegated to Table 3 and never appears in the headline table, inflating the apparent gains. The catastrophic baseline numbers (e.g., GPT-Audio CER 44.679 in the no-history setting) also suggest the baselines may not have been prompted or adapted fairly.

The 'optimal balance' claim is asserted, not demonstrated. The proposed model is strictly dominated on each axis by one of the ablations (content-only has lower CER 0.783, style-only has higher MCLP -4.590); the choice of λ=10, C=15, τ=0.2 is arbitrary and no sensitivity analysis is given. The constant bias C=15 is a within-group constant in GRPO and has no effect on the normalized advantages, so its inclusion is unexplained.

No validation that MCLP isolates *style* from other factors. The argument that 'transcript is identical, so variation must be style' is a non-sequitur; the score can also reflect recording conditions, speaker/timbre, and overall acoustic fidelity. There is no correlation analysis against any independent style measure, and no test of whether MCLP is sensitive to speaker identity or channel.

Presentation and scholarship problems. The bibliography is badly inconsistent (e.g., 'Guo et al. 2023' cited for DeepSeek-R1 (2025); 'Wei et al. 2025' for FLAN (2022); 'Shao et al. 2023' for DeepSeekMath (2024); duplicate 'Guo et al. 2023' entries; multiple references dated 2026 with arXiv IDs like 2601.xxxxx), which raises concerns about citation accuracy. There is also a notation bug in Eq. (5), where the ratio is written as π_θ(ρ_{i,t}|·)/π_θold(ρ_{i,t}|·) instead of using the token o_{i,t}.

Ethics/impact handling is inadequate for this data. The corpus is derived from real YouTube dramas with real speakers (source-separated, re-diarized, annotated with inferred identities) and the paper states the dataset will be open-sourced, yet there is no discussion of copyright, consent, or speaker privacy, and the Impact Statement dismisses societal consequences entirely. The 'internal style classification model' used for RL data filtering is also unspecified.

The subjective study is thin (31 samples, 30 valid responses) and the effect is reported only via MOS; given the objective metric barely moves while MOS swings by >1 point, the internal consistency of the evidence is questionable and the source of the MOS gap (style vs. other quality dimensions) is not disentangled.

strengths: Addresses an important bottleneck in expressive role-play TTS: the lack of objective style metrics and dense reward signals beyond emotion classification or content fidelity.

Proposes MCLP, a simple and interpretable metric that leverages the in-context learning ability of pretrained LALMs by measuring continuation log-probability of ground-truth audio tokens conditioned on candidate audio; the idea is novel and practically appealing.

Provides an information-theoretic motivation linking MCLP to mutual information / conditional entropy, and uses MCLP as a GRPO reward with a gated CER penalty, explicitly demonstrating reward hacking under single-reward optimization.

Constructs a large-scale RP-TTS dataset from WenetSpeech drama videos with scene and character annotations, balanced test splits, and an RL filtering pipeline; this could be a useful resource for the community.

Experiments include both objective metrics (CER, Pinyin WER, MCLP) and subjective MOS, plus a human-metric consistency analysis showing that larger MCLP differences correlate with higher human preference.
Ablations separate SFT and RL effects and compare style-only vs content-only rewards, providing useful evidence that the hybrid reward balances intelligibility and expressiveness.
Training details, hyperparameters, and data construction prompts are largely provided, and the dataset is promised to be open-sourced, supporting reproducibility if released as stated.
weaknesses: MCLP may conflate speaking style with timbre, speaker identity, and acoustic quality: conditioning on the candidate audio and predicting ground-truth audio tokens can reward similarity to the reference voice/acoustic condition, not only role-play style. The paper does not fully isolate this confound for the objective metric, and the claim that MI variation is 'dominated by style' is not empirically verified.

The human evaluation is small: only 31 curated samples and 30 valid annotators, with no human evaluation of the ablation variants. Objective MCLP gains over SFT are modest (e.g., -4.725 to -4.636), so the practical significance of MCLP as a standalone metric remains unclear.

The information-theoretic justification is heuristic rather than rigorous: the approximation E[MCLP] ≈ -H(Zgt|Zeval) + KL(Pdata||Ptheta) relies on the pretrained LALM being a strong density estimator with small KL divergence, which is assumed rather than validated. MCLP is also model-dependent and may be exploitable by the same model family.

Potential reward-model/policy coupling: it is not clearly specified whether the MCLP LALM is a frozen separate model or shares the same base/checkpoints as the policy. If it shares architecture or training data with the policy, reward overfitting or model-specific exploitation could inflate results.

Dataset construction relies heavily on automatic tools and LLM/VLM annotations (DeepSeek-R1, Qwen-VL, pyannote, Demucs) without reported human validation or inter-annotator agreement, so scene/character labels and speaker assignments may contain noise. The resulting dataset quality claims are not fully substantiated.

Ethical and legal issues around using real YouTube drama audio, inferred character profiles, and potential voice cloning/timbre transfer are not discussed. The impact statement is generic and does not address consent, copyright, or privacy risks for real speakers.

Presentation and reproducibility details need improvement: Eq. 5 contains a ratio typo, reference formatting is inconsistent, notation overloads S for both speech session and scene description, and baseline details for GPT-Audio/decoding/version are missing. The work is also evaluated only on Mandarin data, limiting claims of generality.

No explicit limitations section is provided; the paper does not discuss failure cases, out-of-domain generalization, language/timbre robustness, or the cost and environmental impact of 32 H800 GPU training, which are relevant for ICML reproducibility and ethics review.

strengths: Proposes MCLP, a novel objective metric that uses an LALM continuation model to quantify stylistic consistency for role-play TTS, addressing a real gap in style evaluation.

Combines MCLP with a CER-based content constraint in GRPO, with a gating mechanism; the ablation shows that single-reward optimization causes severe reward hacking and that the hybrid reward balances intelligibility and expressiveness.
Constructs WenetSpeech-RP-TTS, a large-scale Mandarin RP-TTS dataset with scene and character annotations, multi-turn dialogue structure, and video-level train/test splitting to reduce leakage.
Includes human subjective evaluation with 50 annotators and reports MOS with confidence intervals, plus a separate MCLP-vs-human-judgment win-rate analysis.
Reports meaningful internal ablations: SFT improves over the base model, RL further improves CER, MCLP, CAM++, Emo2Vec, and MOS, and removing either reward component degrades performance.
The limitations section honestly discusses Mandarin-only evaluation, limited domain coverage, and annotation noise from LLM-generated scene/character descriptions.
Provides detailed dataset statistics, including scene categories, speaker counts, dialogue lengths, and per-category/per-length/per-speaker MCLP breakdowns.
The overall direction is useful and timely: RP-TTS lacks objective style metrics, and a likelihood-based LALM metric plus RL reward is a promising research direction.
weaknesses: The main baseline comparison is not controlled. The proposed model is fine-tuned with SFT on 1,435 hours of in-domain RP-TTS data and then optimized with GRPO, while baselines such as GPT-Audio, MiMo-Audio, and Instruct-TTS systems are used off-the-shelf. Thus, large gains may come from in-domain fine-tuning rather than from MCLP itself. Baselines should be fine-tuned on the same data or compared under matched training conditions.

MCLP validation is thin. The paper reports win-rate bins versus ΔMCLP but omits standard correlation coefficients such as Spearman or Kendall, inter-annotator agreement, and direct comparison with CAM++ or Emo2Vec in predicting human MOS. It is therefore unclear whether MCLP is better than existing proxy metrics.

MCLP may capture speaker/timbre or acoustic continuation cues rather than role-play style. The metric conditions on candidate audio and predicts ground-truth audio tokens; without controls for speaker identity, recording condition, or content, it is unclear whether MCLP measures stylistic consistency or simply acoustic similarity. The claim that the Step-Audio-2 tokenizer biases the metric toward style rather than acoustic details is asserted but not empirically tested.

There is circularity risk: MCLP is both the proposed evaluation metric and the RL reward. Reporting MCLP improvements after explicitly optimizing MCLP is not independent evidence. Human MOS helps, but the MCLP-human alignment may be inflated if evaluated on outputs optimized to maximize MCLP.

Reproducibility is limited. The continuation model is trained on 3 million hours of transcribed speech, but it is not specified whether this includes WenetSpeech or the evaluation videos. If test data overlaps with continuation pretraining, MCLP scores may be inflated. The continuation model, dataset, internal style classifier, and several evaluation components are not clearly released, and the code URL is missing from the manuscript.

The MCLP formulation is not clearly symmetric despite the paper's claim. Using candidate audio as context to predict ground-truth tokens can reward copying or repetitive acoustic patterns rather than adherence to scene/character instructions. The ablation without CER shows MCLP can be hacked into expressive gibberish, but there is no sensitivity analysis over tokenizer, model choice, or continuation training data.

Human evaluation details are incomplete. It is unclear whether MOS mixes with- and without-audio-history settings, how many samples each annotator scored, how randomization was handled, and whether confidence intervals account for multiple comparisons. Only 30 test cases are used, and the MCLP correlation study uses 32 listeners but reports limited procedural detail.

Ethical and legal issues are under-addressed. The dataset is derived from real YouTube drama videos and real actors' voices, with character profiles inferred by LLMs. The paper does not discuss consent, copyright/licensing, dataset redistribution restrictions, or privacy safeguards beyond a brief impact statement. Potential impersonation and misuse risks are acknowledged but not concretely mitigated.

Presentation and statistical rigor need improvement. MCLP improvements are often very small (e.g., -4.849 to -4.636), and Figure 5 indicates near-random win rates when ΔMCLP is below about 0.1, while several main comparisons fall in that range. No significance tests are reported for objective metrics, and some figures/tables lack clarity (e.g., how ΔMCLP bins handle negative values).

strengths: Addresses an important and timely problem: maintaining expressive stylistic consistency in multi-turn role-play TTS, where objective metrics and reward signals are genuinely lacking.

Proposes MCLP, a conceptually interesting reward/metric that leverages an LALM's continuation likelihood over speech tokens; integrating it with GRPO and a CER-based content constraint is a reasonable RL design.
Constructs a large-scale RP-TTS dataset from WenetSpeech drama videos with scene and character annotations, video-level train/test splitting, and substantial multi-turn dialogue data.
Includes both objective and subjective evaluations, with MOS scores and a human pairwise win-rate analysis attempting to validate MCLP against human stylistic judgments.
Ablation studies are informative: they show SFT and RL gains, and explicitly expose reward hacking when optimizing MCLP alone (CER > 50%, MOS 1.145), motivating the hybrid reward.
The paper acknowledges several limitations, including Mandarin-only evaluation, domain coverage, and LLM-generated annotation noise.
The proposed model outperforms several strong baselines, including multi-turn LALMs and Instruct-TTS systems, across CER, CAM++, Emo2Vec, MCLP, and MOS in the reported tables.
weaknesses: The core construct validity of MCLP is not established. Conditioning on candidate audio to predict ground-truth audio tokens can reflect acoustic continuation, speaker/timbre similarity, recording conditions, tokenizer artifacts, or general fluency rather than role-play style. No probing or controlled experiments isolate style from these confounds.

Circular evaluation: MCLP is used directly as the RL reward and then reported as a central objective improvement. The highest MCLP score is expected by construction and does not independently demonstrate better stylistic consistency.

The human validation of MCLP is weak. It reports only pairwise win rates binned by ΔMCLP, without correlation coefficients, statistical significance, confidence intervals for MCLP, or comparisons against alternative style metrics. Main-table MCLP differences are small (~0.1–0.2) and lack uncertainty estimates.

The ablation reveals that MCLP alone can be hacked into repetitive gibberish with CER > 50% and MOS 1.145, undermining its validity as a style metric. The CER gate is a heuristic patch rather than a principled solution to reward hacking.

Subjective evaluation is confounded: several baselines and even ground truth are marked as resynthesized via the Step-Audio-2 tokenizer using ground-truth audio prompts, which may alter style/timbre and favor the Step-Audio-2-based proposed model. Blinding, annotator consistency, and sample selection are insufficiently documented.

Baseline comparisons are not fully fair. Instruct-TTS systems are evaluated only without audio history and with rewritten prompts; several baselines are not fine-tuned on RP-TTS data; GPT-Audio is closed-source; and model/data scale differences are not controlled.

Reproducibility is limited. The code URL is missing/blank in the manuscript, the dataset likely cannot be released due to YouTube/drama copyright, and the pipeline depends on proprietary or internal models (DeepSeek-R1, Qwen-VL-7B, internal style classifier, Step-Audio-2 ASR). The 3M-hour continuation training and RL setup lack sufficient detail.
Dataset statistics are inconsistent: Table 1 reports 311,938 filtered scenes, while Table 5 reports 304,489 training scenes plus 900 test scenes = 305,389, leaving 6,549 scenes unexplained.

Ethical and legal issues are under-addressed. The dataset derives from real drama videos and voices, raising copyright, consent, and impersonation concerns; the impact statement mentions watermarking but provides no concrete safeguards or licensing discussion.
The claim that MCLP is 'interpretable' is unsupported. A log-probability score is not inherently interpretable, and no latent-space analysis or qualitative probe demonstrates what it captures.

Presentation and technical details are incomplete: the choice of context order [w, z_eval, w] is justified only informally, with no ablation of order, no-audio, or repeated-transcript alternatives; the repeated transcript may let the model rely on text rather than candidate style.

The limitations section is honest but incomplete: it does not discuss the metric-hacking risk, subjective-evaluation confounds, copyright/consent issues, or the lack of independent validation for MCLP.

strengths: Proposes MCLP, a novel and interpretable objective metric that uses LALM in-context continuation likelihood to quantify stylistic consistency, and validates it against human pairwise preferences with a clear positive trend (Figure 5).

Constructs WenetSpeech-RP-TTS, a large-scale multi-turn role-play TTS dataset with scene and character annotations, video-level train/test split, and useful statistics; this is a substantial resource for the community.

Provides a complete SFT+GRPO pipeline with a gated hybrid reward combining MCLP and CER; ablation studies (Table 3) convincingly show that optimizing either reward alone leads to reward hacking or degraded style, while the hybrid achieves the best balance.

Empirical results (Table 2) show consistent gains over strong LALM and Instruct-TTS baselines across CER, CAM++, Emo2Vec, MCLP, and MOS in both with- and without-audio-history settings; Appendix B also provides preliminary cross-lingual evidence.
Includes an honest limitations discussion and impact statement, acknowledging Mandarin-only data, domain coverage, automatic annotation noise, and misuse risks.
weaknesses: The central claim that MCLP measures stylistic consistency is not fully disentangled from acoustic, timbre, or speaker similarity. The reverse continuation likelihood uses the candidate audio as context for predicting ground-truth audio, and the paper offers only a conceptual symmetry argument without empirical validation. No analysis controls for speaker/timbre or shows that MCLP is insensitive to these factors.

The paper does not compare MCLP as an RL reward against alternative style rewards (e.g., emotion-classifier rewards or other continuous style metrics), despite claiming that emotion-based rewards are inadequate. This makes the reward-design contribution less convincing.

Reproducibility is limited: MCLP depends on a continuation model trained on 3 million hours of speech, and it is unclear whether these weights or the exact training setup will be released. The code URL is incomplete in the manuscript, and the subjective evaluation uses only 30 test cases with 48 valid annotators, with no inter-annotator agreement reported.

Evaluation details raise fairness and robustness concerns: some baselines are marked as resynthesized via the Step-Audio-2 tokenizer while the proposed model is not, and MCLP differences in Table 2 are small with no significance tests. There is also no sensitivity analysis for reward hyperparameters C, λ, and τ.

Dataset and annotation concerns: scene descriptions and character profiles are automatically generated by LLMs, which may introduce noise or bias. The dataset is derived from WenetSpeech/YouTube drama content, but licensing, privacy, and consent issues are not discussed in depth.
